chapters.title: Chapter 3: Sourcing Alternative Data: Vendors, Costs, and Compliance

lessons.title: SEBI Regulations, Data Privacy, and Ethical Boundaries in Alt Data Use

body.text: Every compliance thread in this course so far, UPSI, DPDP, RBI payment rules, has been touched in passing. This lesson turns those threads into one operating framework a desk can actually run.

children.text: You have already met the UPSI test, India's DPDP Act, and RBI's payment data rules in earlier lessons, each time attached to the specific data category being discussed. This lesson pulls back to the full regulatory picture: where SEBI's rulebook touches an alt-data desk directly, what registration category actually governs what you do with a signal, how data privacy obligations escalate as you scale, and where the honest answer to 'is this legal' is yes but the right question is still 'should we do it anyway.'
Where SEBI's Rulebook Actually Touches Alternative Data

body.caption: Three areas of SEBI regulation an alt-data quant desk needs to track

cells: Trading on or tipping others with UPSI
The compliance test from Chapter 1: any data source depending on an insider's breach of duty is UPSI, not alternative data, regardless of the vendor's framing
Approval and tagging of systematic trading strategies deployed through exchange infrastructure

A strategy fed by alternative data is still a systematic strategy, and SEBI's oversight of algorithmic trading has historically extended over time to cover a wider set of participants, not just the largest institutional desks
Who needs to register as what, depending on the activity
Trading pooled capital, publishing research, and giving personalized advice are three different regulated activities, covered next

children.text: The Registration Question: What Are You Actually Doing With This Signal?

Chapter 1 mapped four buy-side users of alternative data: hedge funds and PMS, prop desks, sell-side research teams, and larger AMCs. Each of those roles maps to a different SEBI registration category, and the registration follows what you do with the signal's output, not how sophisticated the underlying data science is.

body.title: What You Do With the Signal Decides Your Registration

columns.label: Trading Pooled or Managed Capital
points: Running the signal inside a fund that manages other people's money
Falls under SEBI's Portfolio Managers Regulations or Alternative Investment Fund Regulations, depending on structure
A pure proprietary desk trading only its own firm's capital typically sits outside this specific category

columns.label: Publishing Research or Personalized Advice
points: Publishing a data-driven tracker or report for clients falls under SEBI's Research Analysts Regulations
Giving personalized buy or sell recommendations based on the signal falls under SEBI's Investment Advisers Regulations
This applies even if the underlying insight came from a satellite image or a web scrape rather than a spreadsheet of ratios

children.text: The recurring mistake is treating alternative data as a technical novelty that sits outside the existing regulatory map. It does not. A VAHAN-based auto tracker published for institutional clients is research under SEBI's framework in exactly the same way a P/E-based note is, and the sophistication of the underlying data source changes none of that.
Data Privacy Escalation: From DPDP Basics to Significant Data Fiduciary

markDefs.definition: A category under India's DPDP Act, 2023, that the government may designate for certain data fiduciaries based on factors such as the volume and sensitivity of personal data they process. Entities notified under this category face heavier obligations, including appointing a Data Protection Officer and conducting periodic Data Protection Impact Assessments.

children.text: You have already seen the DPDP Act's core natural-person test applied to scraping, geolocation, and payment data. The Act also has an escalation ladder: entities processing personal data at large enough volume or sensitivity can be designated a

, which brings heavier obligations than a smaller-scale processor faces. A quant desk running a handful of anonymized, aggregated panels is unlikely to sit anywhere near this threshold today, but a desk building a large in-house geolocation or payment data operation, exactly the kind of ambitious build-vs-buy project covered later in this chapter, should track this escalation ladder before it scales, not after a regulator asks about it.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Regulatory Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: A SEBI-registered category for managing investment portfolios on behalf of clients under a discretionary or non-discretionary mandate.
A SEBI-registered pooled investment vehicle structure, commonly used by quant and hedge-fund-style strategies raising money from sophisticated investors.
A SEBI-registered category required to publish investment research, including data-driven trackers and reports, for clients.
A DPDP Act, 2023, designation for entities processing personal data at a scale or sensitivity that triggers extra obligations, such as appointing a Data Protection Officer.

children.text: The Ethics Beyond the Letter of the Law: Don't Break What Citizens Rely On

Much of this course points you toward public government portals: VAHAN, the e-way bill system, MCA21. These systems were built to serve citizens and businesses conducting ordinary government transactions, not to feed a hedge fund's data pipeline. Polling any of them aggressively enough to degrade performance for the actual public users of that system is legal in most cases, but it is not the kind of behaviour a responsible market participant should engage in, and it invites exactly the kind of regulatory and reputational attention that gets an entire data category shut down for everyone.

body.title: The Junior Engineer's Real-Time Idea
body.scenario: A junior engineer on your desk proposes polling the VAHAN registration dashboard once every second, across all state RTOs simultaneously, to catch registration updates as close to real time as possible and gain a speed edge over any competitor using a slower, hourly refresh.
body.prompt: What is wrong with this plan, separate from whether it would technically work, and what would you propose instead?
body.modelAnswer: Polling a shared public government system once per second across every state RTO simultaneously is aggressive enough to meaningfully add load to infrastructure that ordinary citizens and businesses rely on for genuine transactions, and vehicle registrations do not actually update at sub-second frequency in a way that justifies this cost, so the plan buys almost no real informational edge for a real risk of degrading a public service. The better approach is to profile how frequently the underlying data actually changes, most likely on the order of hours rather than seconds, and set a polling interval that comfortably captures that update frequency without needlessly hammering the server, along with proper caching so you never re-fetch data you already have. This protects the public system, reduces the chance of being rate-limited or blocked entirely, which would end the data source for your desk, and still gets you effectively all of the achievable timeliness edge.

children.text: Building an Internal Alt Data Compliance Program

body.title: A Minimum Viable Compliance Program for an Alt Data Desk
steps: Designate a specific compliance owner for data sourcing decisions, not a shared, ambiguous responsibility
Maintain a data source registry documenting where every dataset feeding a live signal came from, and the compliance basis for using it
Run the UPSI compliance test from Chapter 1 on every new source before it reaches a researcher's laptop, not after a signal is already built on it
Review each vendor's own compliance representations periodically, not only at the point of initial onboarding
Train researchers specifically on UPSI risk in an alternative data context, since the risk looks different from classic insider trading scenarios and is easy to miss
Keep an internal channel where a researcher who suspects a data source might be improper can raise it without penalty for having asked

body.text: A good alt data compliance program is boring by design: a registry, a designated owner, a training slide, a checklist run before a new source goes live. The desks that get into trouble are rarely the ones following a boring process. They are the ones who treated compliance as something to check after the signal already worked.

This lesson explains general regulatory concepts for education and is not legal or compliance advice. SEBI's rules, the DPDP Act's implementing provisions, and related frameworks continue to evolve, so consult qualified legal counsel and your compliance function before relying on any of this for an actual business decision.

points: SEBI's insider trading regulations, algorithmic trading framework, and intermediary registration categories all apply to alternative-data-driven strategies exactly as they apply to traditional ones
What you do with a signal, trade pooled capital, publish research, or give personalized advice, decides which SEBI registration category applies, not how sophisticated the underlying data is

India's DPDP Act has an escalation ladder: entities processing personal data at large enough scale can be designated a Significant Data Fiduciary with heavier obligations, including a Data Protection Officer and Data Protection Impact Assessments
Aggressively polling shared public infrastructure like VAHAN, the e-way bill system, or MCA21 can be legal yet still irresponsible, since it risks degrading a service ordinary citizens depend on
A responsible polling strategy matches request frequency to how often the underlying data actually changes, plus caching, rather than maximizing speed for its own sake
A minimum viable compliance program needs a designated owner, a data source registry, pre-use UPSI testing, periodic vendor review, targeted training, and a safe internal reporting channel
